profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting between the SECOHealth ingestion pipeline lead and the cross-site analytics lead to align the handoff for the next internal ecosystem-health snapshot. The team is preparing a shared dataset and summary package that combines package-registry signals, issue activity, and maintainer-network features from partner institutions in Montreal, Mons, and Laval. The immediate context is that a draft internal snapshot must be ready before a cross-university methods review next week, and both workstreams depend on each other: one team exports the normalized ecosystem snapshot, while the other computes the interdisciplinary indicators and assembles a review-ready summary. The agenda is to confirm what will be delivered in the next snapshot, where the shared artifact will live, what version/baseline it should use, and what 'ready for review' means for the handoff. The expected outcome is surface-level agreement on the snapshot handoff, analytics timing, and ownership of the shared package for the review meeting.

members.name: Nadia Bouchard
members.expertise: Research data pipelines, software repository mining, schema versioning, reproducible ETL workflows
members.background: Based at Polytechnique Montreal, Nadia maintains the shared ingestion and normalization jobs that collect ecosystem signals from GitHub, package registries, and mailing-list mirrors used by the project.
members.private_state: She wants to keep the handoff lightweight so her team can stabilize a recent schema migration before the review, and she is trying to avoid reopening older partner-specific edge cases that would delay the export.
hidden_assumptions: When people ask for the 'snapshot', they mean the normalized monthly export generated from the canonical ETL pipeline, not any downstream enriched derivative.
The 'current baseline' is the latest pipeline run on schema v3.2, even if some partner notebooks still target the previous feature names.
If a package is 'ready for review', it means the files are internally consistent, checks passed, and the data dictionary is attached; interpretive visual polish can happen later.
The shared deliverable lives in the project S3 bucket under the standard snapshot path, and downstream teams pull from there rather than editing a collaborative folder.
Coverage notes apply only to the core GitHub and package-registry entities defined in the export contract, not optional maintainer-affiliation enrichments.

members.name: Julien Maréchal
members.expertise: Empirical software engineering, socio-technical indicators, cross-site synthesis, research reporting
members.background: Based at the University of Mons, Julien coordinates the indicator notebooks and the package that will be shown to the interdisciplinary methods group, integrating inputs from multiple institutions.
members.private_state: He wants a review package that his collaborators can open directly without extra wrangling, and he is worried that any mismatch across sites will make the indicators look immature during the methods review.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'snapshot', they mean the analyst-facing bundle that already includes the standard enrichments and column names expected by the indicator notebooks.
The 'current baseline' is the last review-approved snapshot lineage from April, with only additive updates, because comparability matters more than adopting the newest schema immediately.
If something is 'ready for review', it should be directly usable in the slide deck and shared notebooks, including stable labels, derived summary tables, and no manual translation step.
The shared package should live in the common Nextcloud review folder so partner researchers can annotate and reuse the exact same files.
Coverage notes include maintainer-affiliation and institutional-link fields because the socio-technical indicators depend on them even if those fields are produced later in the pipeline.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that Nadia will deliver 'the snapshot' by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the canonical normalized export from the ETL pipeline: raw-to-cleaned entities, standard IDs, and core metrics only.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the analyst-facing bundle: normalized export plus standard enrichments, notebook-compatible labels, and derived tables used by the indicators team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both teams routinely say 'snapshot' as if it were a single obvious artifact, and because each usually receives a package from an intermediary script, neither thinks to unpack the exact contents during a short coordination call.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to stay on the 'current baseline' for the review package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the most recent successful pipeline baseline: schema v3.2 with renamed contributor-role fields and updated package identity joins from the June run.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the previously review-approved April baseline that the cross-site notebooks and draft figures were built on.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'current baseline' sounds like a stabilizing choice rather than a point of ambiguity, and both have a legitimate recent baseline in mind from their own workflow, so neither expects the other to mean a different one.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the package should be 'ready for review' before the methods meeting.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'ready for review' means technically validated delivery: schema checks pass, row counts reconcile, and documentation notes known gaps.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'ready for review' means presentation-usable delivery: the package runs in shared notebooks, summary tables are precomputed, and collaborators can inspect outputs without extra adaptation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a shared project milestone, but each role naturally measures readiness using the standards of their own downstream obligations, and in a cooperative meeting both hear confirmation rather than discrepancy.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the files will go into the 'shared review package' for everyone to use.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to publish immutable files to the S3 snapshot location and send the path; any transformed review materials are downstream responsibilities.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects the package to be placed and maintained in the collaborative Nextcloud review folder with final filenames, where minor fixes can be swapped in and partners can work from the same visible copy.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the goal of one shared package, but each assumes the standard tool and ownership pattern of their own workstream; because both storage locations are familiar project resources, the mismatch sounds operationally trivial and goes unspoken.
